commonMistakes: Use extension, not total spring length, in the equation.
Convert centimetres or millimetres to metres when required.
Do not use ½ke² blindly if the spring is clearly outside the region where the stated model applies.

detailedExplanation: Verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Physics Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and aligned to AQA GCSE Physics 8463.
For a spring that obeys Hooke’s law, elastic potential energy can be calculated using Eₑ = ½ke². An equivalent form is Eₑ = ½Fe when F = ke applies.
The energy stored corresponds to the work done stretching or compressing the spring. On a force–extension graph, it is represented by the area under the graph.
Because extension is squared in Eₑ = ½ke², doubling extension within the Hooke’s-law region makes the elastic energy four times larger.
The equation is applied within the region where the spring behaves elastically as assumed. Beyond proportional or elastic limits, the simple model may no longer describe the spring accurately.
examTips: If force and extension are given, ½Fe can be quickest; if k and extension are given, use ½ke².
